lead: This unit is about the second phase of a compiler: the parser. It shows how a context-free grammar becomes a parse tree, how to rewrite a grammar so a parser can work top-down, and how an LL(1) parser uses FIRST, FOLLOW and a parsing table. After it you can build and trace a predictive parser and recover from syntax errors without stopping at the first bad token.
about: The unit follows one token stream from the lexer to a parse tree. Chapter 2.1 places the parser in the compiler and defines syntax errors. Chapter 2.2 gives the grammar machinery: derivations, sentential forms and parse trees. Chapter 2.3 repairs grammars by removing ambiguity, left recursion and common prefixes. Chapter 2.4 turns a repaired grammar into recursive descent procedures. Chapter 2.5 computes FIRST and FOLLOW sets; only a few universities teach it as a separate topic. Chapter 2.6 uses those sets to fill an LL(1) table and run the predictive parsing algorithm. Chapter 2.7 adds panic-mode recovery so a bad token does not end the compile.

chapters.idea: The parser checks that the token stream follows a grammar and builds a parse tree, reporting syntax errors instead of silently guessing.
chapters.depth: Position after lexical analysis; input tokens, output parse tree or its trace. Show the parser's two jobs: recognition and tree building. Cover syntax error categories: lexical (misspelled keyword), syntactic (missing semicolon), semantic (type mismatch) — note semantic is Unit 4. Error handling goals: report clearly, recover, not loop. Mention strategies in one line: panic mode, phrase level, error productions, global correction; details in 2.7. Some syllabi call this 'role of the parser' or 'syntax analyzer'.

figure.title: Where the parser sits
figure.aria: The parser receives a token stream and produces a parse tree, with a side path to error handling and a dashed lookup into the symbol table.

chapters.example: A C statement int x = 3 is lexed to tokens: keyword int, identifier x, assign, number 3, semicolon. The parser accepts it with the declaration grammar. Change it to int = 3; and the parser reports a syntax error at token =: an identifier was expected.
chapters.trap: Treating a parser error as a compiler crash; or blaming the parser for a type error that belongs to semantic analysis.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 for tokens, lexemes and the compiler phase diagram.
chapters.leave: Lexical scanning and regular expressions to Unit 1; semantic checks to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: A context-free grammar generates strings by derivations, and a parse tree records which production rewrote each nonterminal.
chapters.depth: Define CFG as (V, T, P, S): nonterminals, terminals, productions, start symbol. Define leftmost and rightmost derivation, sentential form, yield, parse tree, ambiguity maybe mention but leave to 2.3. Show that a leftmost derivation and a parse tree correspond one-to-one. Distinguish the language generated by a grammar from the parse tree for one string. Some syllabi say 'derivations and parse trees' only.

figure.aria: A parse tree for id + id * id: the root E splits into E + T, the left E reduces to id, and the right T splits into T * F with both sides reducing to id.

chapters.example: Grammar: E → E + T | T, T → T * F | F, F → id | ( E ). For the string id + id * id, give the leftmost derivation E ⇒ E + T ⇒ T + T ⇒ F + T ⇒ id + T ⇒ id + T * F ⇒ id + F * F ⇒ id + id * F ⇒ id + id * id and draw the parse tree.
chapters.trap: Confusing a derivation step with a parse tree node, or using a rightmost derivation when the question asks for leftmost; also drawing the tree for the wrong grammar, since operator precedence changes the tree.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 tokens; basic sets and strings.
chapters.leave: Ambiguity and grammar repair to 2.3; attribute evaluation to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: A grammar that is ambiguous, left-recursive or not left-factored can break a top-down parser, so rewrite it into an equivalent grammar for the same language.
chapters.depth: Ambiguity: two parse trees for one string; dangling else example. Removing ambiguity is not algorithmic in general; use precedence, associativity or restructuring. Left recursion: immediate A → Aα | β becomes A → βA′, A′ → αA′ | ε; indirect left recursion algorithm by ordering nonterminals. Left factoring: A → αβ₁ | αβ₂ becomes A → αA′, A′ → β₁ | β₂. Mention that these transformations preserve language but not parse tree shape. Some syllabi call it 'elimination of left recursion' and 'left factoring'.

figure.title: Left recursion removal
figure.aria: The left-recursive rule A → Aα | β is rewritten as A → βA′, then A′ → αA′ and A′ → ε carry the repetition.

chapters.example: Remove left recursion from E → E + T | T and T → T * F | F, giving E → T E′, E′ → + T E′ | ε and T → F T′, T′ → * F T′ | ε. Then left-factor S → i E t S | i E t S e S | a, giving S → i E t S S′ | a and S′ → e S | ε.
chapters.trap: Dropping the ε production from A′, or left-factoring only the first two alternatives and leaving a third with the same prefix; also applying left-recursion removal to a rule that is not left-recursive.
chapters.leave: Ambiguity detection theory and LR conflict resolution to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: A recursive descent parser is a set of procedures, one per nonterminal, that tries productions in order and consumes tokens as it goes.
chapters.depth: Top-down parsing builds the tree from root to leaves. Recursive descent with backtracking: try each production, save the token position, restore on failure. Predictive (non-backtracking) recursive descent when FIRST sets are disjoint. Show code shape: procedure E() calls T(); then E′(); match(token). Explain match and lookahead. Mention left recursion causes infinite recursion, so 2.3 must run first. LL(1) means left-to-right scan, leftmost derivation, one token lookahead. Some syllabi call it 'recursive descent parser' and 'predictive parser' separately.

figure.aria: A call tree for recursive descent: E() calls T(), T() calls F(), F() matches id, and E′ handles the plus and the next T().

chapters.example: Using E → T E′, E′ → + T E′ | ε, T → F T′, T′ → * F T′ | ε, F → id | ( E ), trace recursive descent on id + id * id. Show the call sequence E → T → F → match(id) → T′ → ε → E′ → match(+) → T → F → match(id) and so on.
chapters.trap: Writing a procedure that calls itself on the same token because the grammar is left-recursive; or forgetting to advance the input pointer in match.
chapters.leave: Table-driven LL(1) to 2.6; bottom-up parsing to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: FIRST(α) is the set of terminals that can begin a string derived from α; FOLLOW(A) is the set of terminals that can appear immediately after A in some sentential form.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach FIRST and FOLLOW as a separate exam topic; most fold it into 2.6. Define nullable. Compute FIRST for terminals, nonterminals and strings: add FIRST of the first symbol, continue while nullable. Compute FOLLOW: start symbol gets $; for A → αBβ add FIRST(β) minus ε to FOLLOW(B); if β is nullable add FOLLOW(A). Show the iterative fixed point. Mention ε handling.

figure.title: FIRST and FOLLOW for the expression grammar
figure.aria: Rows show the FIRST and FOLLOW sets for E, E′ and T, with the dollar and epsilon marks picked out.

chapters.example: For E → T E′, E′ → + T E′ | ε, T → F T′, T′ → * F T′ | ε, F → id | ( E ), compute FIRST and FOLLOW for every nonterminal. Answers: FIRST(E)=FIRST(T)=FIRST(F)={ (, id }; FIRST(E′)={ +, ε }; FIRST(T′)={ *, ε }; FOLLOW(E)=FOLLOW(E′)={ ), $ }; FOLLOW(T)=FOLLOW(T′)={ +, ), $ }; FOLLOW(F)={ *, +, ), $ }.
chapters.trap: Putting ε into FIRST of a nonterminal but not treating it as nullable when computing FOLLOW; or forgetting $ on the start symbol.
chapters.leave: Table construction to 2.6; formal LL(1) proofs are not needed here.

chapters.idea: An LL(1) parser is a stack machine driven by a two-dimensional table M[nonterminal, terminal], where each entry is the production to apply.
chapters.depth: Construction: for A → α, for each a in FIRST(α) put A → α in M[A,a]; if α is nullable, for each b in FOLLOW(A) put A → α in M[A,b]. Conflicts mean the grammar is not LL(1). Predictive parsing algorithm: stack starts with $S, input ends with $; look at X on top and a as lookahead; if X=a=$ accept; if X=a pop; if X is a nonterminal use M[X,a]; if empty error. Show parse trace columns: stack, input, action. Some syllabi call it 'predictive parser', 'LL(1) parser' or 'table-driven parser'.

figure.title: LL(1) parser loop
figure.aria: The parser reads the stack top X and lookahead a, looks up M[X,a], then pushes a production, matches a terminal, accepts, or reports an error.

chapters.example: Grammar: E → T E′, E′ → + T E′ | ε, T → F T′, T′ → * F T′ | ε, F → id | ( E ). Build the LL(1) table. Then parse id + id * id $ and give the first six stack, input and action rows. First rows: $E, id + id * id $, output E → T E′; $E′T, id + id * id $, output T → F T′; $E′T′F, id + id * id $, output F → id; $E′T′id, id + id * id $, match id; $E′T′, + id * id $, output T′ → ε; $E′, + id * id $, output E′ → + T E′.
chapters.trap: Putting a nullable production under FIRST only and forgetting FOLLOW; or filling M[A,a] twice and ignoring the conflict.
chapters.prereq: 2.5 FIRST and FOLLOW sets, 2.3 repaired grammar, 2.4 procedure view.
chapters.leave: LR tables to Unit 3; semantic actions to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: When a predictive parser finds an empty table entry it reports the error and uses FOLLOW sets and token skipping to resume at a synchronising token.
chapters.depth: Error detection at an empty M entry. Panic mode: if the lookahead is in FOLLOW(A), pop A; else skip tokens until a token in FOLLOW(A) or in FIRST of some open nonterminal. Phrase-level recovery: insert or delete a token, such as a missing semicolon. Error productions: add A → error α to the grammar. Global correction is too costly; mention only. Show that recovery must guarantee progress to avoid infinite loops. Some syllabi call it 'error recovery in predictive parsing'.

figure.title: Panic-mode recovery
figure.aria: An empty table entry triggers an error report; the parser pops the nonterminal if the lookahead is in its FOLLOW set, otherwise it skips tokens and checks again.

chapters.example: Use the LL(1) table of 2.6 and parse id + * id $. After matching +, the stack is $E′T and the input is * id $. M[T,*] is empty. FOLLOW(T)={ +, ), $ }, so * is not a synchronising token: skip *. The next lookahead id is in FIRST(T), so apply T → F T′ and continue. The stray * is discarded and parsing resumes.
chapters.trap: Skipping a token but not changing the stack, so the parser loops on the same entry; or skipping tokens that are valid starts of the remaining input.
chapters.leave: LR error recovery to Unit 3; semantic error messages to Unit 4.
